lines.text: Can a machine learn malaria's chemical signature, and does it still work on data it has never seen?
Malaria infected an estimated 282 million people in 2024 and killed 610,000.
Progress has stalled, parasite gene deletions can defeat rapid tests, and funding falls billions short.
Metabolomics measures the small molecules in blood: amino acids, vitamins, lipids.
Infection changes the mix, and that chemical fingerprint is a window into what the body is doing.
Machine learning can search that fingerprint for patterns.
But with hundreds of molecules and only a few hundred samples, a model can simply memorise what it has seen.
Memorising isn't learning.
We used two public serum datasets from children in Burkina Faso: 305 samples, 220 metabolites measured in both.
Many samples are repeat visits by the same child, so this is not 305 independent people.
The data is log-scaled, normalised, gap-filled and standardised.
Even then the two datasets sit on separate islands, a technical gap.
A statistical correction can merge them in a picture, but we used it only as a diagnostic.
Two hundred and twenty candidates is too many.
So two different methods, one linear, one tree-based, each vote.
Only metabolites both pick survive.
Here's the honest test.
Train on one whole dataset, test on the other, which the model has never seen, then swap.
Cleaning, selection and tuning are learned from the training data alone.
No peeking.
While tuning, models scored up to 0.99 AUC, where 0.5 is a coin flip and 1 is perfect.
On the unseen dataset they landed between 0.50 and 0.70.
Logistic regression and a heavily tuned XGBoost both averaged about 0.64.
More tuning didn't close the gap.
That gap is the finding.
Fit on all the data, the same selection leaves eleven metabolites.
The strongest three: phenylalanine, pointing up; sphingosine-1-phosphate and retinol, down.
Each fits published malaria literature, which makes them worth a biologist's attention, not a discovery.
An open-source demo takes the eleven values and explains each prediction.
A research illustration, not a diagnostic.
So this is a transparent, reusable workflow and a short list for expert review.
Not a validated panel, not a diagnostic, and not new knowledge about malaria in Indonesia.
Next: independent cohorts, targeted confirmation, and prospective local studies.
A modest result, and a method you can trust.
